summary: Independently authored English narrative draft for the Cuban Missile Crisis case (not a translation of the Korean submission).

narrative.hook: A launch site is taking shape ninety miles from your coast. It isn't finished. Strike now and you might destroy it before it is. Strike now and you might also start the war you're trying to prevent.
narrative.short_setup: In October 1962, U.S. reconnaissance photographs confirm Soviet medium-range ballistic missile sites under construction in Cuba. The missiles are not yet operational, but no one can say with confidence how many days that will remain true. For a week, a small group meets almost continuously in the White House basement, weighing two live options: strike the sites now by air, or impose a naval blockade and buy time to negotiate. Either path risks a direct collision between two nuclear powers.
narrative.why_option_a_made_sense: The Joint Chiefs of Staff, and Air Force Chief of Staff Curtis LeMay in particular, pushed hard for an immediate air strike. Intelligence held that the missiles were not yet ready to fire, but nobody could say how long that window would stay open -- every day of delay moved the sites closer to completion. Militarily, a strike went straight at the source of the problem: destroy the missiles themselves rather than negotiate around them. In the security logic of the Cold War, a fast, overwhelming response to an unambiguous military provocation was widely seen as the move that actually deterred further escalation, not the one that risked it.
narrative.why_option_b_made_sense: Attorney General Robert Kennedy and Defense Secretary Robert McNamara argued from a different premise: if the missiles weren't yet operational, there was no military emergency that required striking today. A surprise attack, by contrast, carried real costs -- it would look to much of the world like a reverse Pearl Harbor, and any Soviet casualties would make de-escalation far harder to manage afterward. A blockade let Khrushchev choose whether to test a publicly drawn line, gave Washington time to see how Moscow would respond, and kept the harder options -- strike, invasion -- available if diplomacy failed.
narrative.actual_decision_explanation: On the evening of October 20, 1962, after a week of near-continuous ExComm deliberation, Kennedy chose the naval blockade. He announced it publicly on October 22. The decision rested on the intelligence assessment that the missiles weren't yet operational, concern about the diplomatic and moral cost of a surprise attack, and a judgment that this route left Khrushchev room to step back without being cornered. The blockade still needed a legal basis -- the administration secured it through the Rio Treaty and the Organization of American States -- and allied governments had to be briefed before the speech aired.
narrative.outcome_story: On October 28, Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles under United Nations verification. In exchange, the United States publicly pledged not to invade Cuba, and privately agreed to withdraw its own aging Jupiter missiles from Turkey -- a trade it insisted on keeping out of the public record. By late November the missiles were dismantled and shipped out, and the blockade was lifted once the withdrawal of Soviet bombers was also confirmed. In the crisis's aftermath, a direct communications link between Washington and Moscow was established, and the episode fed into the momentum toward the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty -- though those later developments had other causes too, not this crisis alone.
narrative.hindsight_analysis: It's tempting to read the outcome backward and call the blockade the obviously correct call. But the people in that room were working with real gaps in what they knew. Nuclear warheads had, in fact, already reached Cuba -- the reconnaissance photos showed launch pads, not confirmation of what was or wasn't already armed. Soviet troop strength on the island was four to five times larger than U.S. intelligence estimated. And on October 27, deep in the blockade, the Soviet submarine B-59 -- under depth-charge pressure from U.S. destroyers and cut off from Moscow -- came within one dissenting officer's vote of launching a nuclear torpedo; unanimous consent among three officers was required, and Vasily Arkhipov withheld his. Nobody in the White House knew that moment was happening. So the tidy story -- good decision, good outcome, therefore proven right -- is only half true. The blockade itself was a carefully reasoned choice given what was knowable at the time: it lowered the odds of immediate escalation and kept a path to reversal open. That earns it a strong decision-quality rating on its own terms. But whether it actually ended without war also depended on things Washington neither planned for nor controlled. The reverse counterfactual holds too -- there's no way to prove a strike would have guaranteed war. What this case demonstrates isn't a correct answer; it's the value of preserving a way to reverse course when you're deciding under incomplete information.
narrative.decision_principle: When choosing between a strong move that resolves things now and a weaker move that keeps your options reversible, the strong move usually feels more decisive. Under genuine uncertainty, though, preserving the ability to change course can be the more powerful strategy.
narrative.longform_story:
On the morning of October 16, 1962, National Security Adviser McGeorge Bundy walked into President Kennedy's bedroom carrying photo-analysis from a U-2 reconnaissance flight taken two days earlier. Near San Cristobal, Cuba, the Soviet Union was building medium-range ballistic missile launch sites.

That moment is this story's T0. Nothing had been decided yet. Nothing had been said publicly yet. Kennedy needed options, and he needed them fast.

What he could actually confirm was this: photo interpretation showed the launch pads were unfinished, and intelligence estimated they could become operational within days to weeks -- an estimate, not a fixed deadline. Just two days earlier, Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko had told Kennedy directly, in the Oval Office, that Soviet aid to Cuba was purely defensive training assistance. The Soviets were lying, and Kennedy was looking straight at the lie.

Kennedy immediately convened a small circle of top advisers -- the group that would become known as ExComm. For the next week, they met in the White House basement almost every day.

The argument split into two main camps.

One was immediate air strikes, pressed hardest by the Joint Chiefs of Staff and Air Force Chief of Staff Curtis LeMay. The logic was straightforward: if the missiles weren't operational yet, this might be the last window to destroy them before they were. Every day of delay only moved completion closer. Militarily, a strike was the most direct fix -- eliminate the source of the problem rather than negotiate around it.

The other was a naval blockade, championed by Robert Kennedy and Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, built on a different premise. If the missiles couldn't yet fire, there was no military emergency requiring an attack today. The real risk, in this view, sat in the political and moral register: a surprise strike with no warning could be read internationally as a reverse Pearl Harbor, and any Soviet military deaths would make containing the fallout far harder.

Both options had real backing. Both were executable. And both carried a risk that, misjudged, could put two nuclear powers into direct confrontation.

Even inside the Joint Chiefs, no one could guarantee a strike would destroy every missile site outright. Some sites might survive -- and if they did, the possibility that the Soviets would actually fire what remained couldn't be ruled out. ExComm was already aware of that uncertainty as it debated.

On the evening of October 20, Kennedy chose the blockade. The decision combined the intelligence judgment that the missiles weren't yet operational, concern over the moral cost of a surprise attack, and a calculation that this route left Khrushchev a way to back down without losing face. But a blockade couldn't just be announced as a military maneuver -- under international law it could itself be read as an act of war, so the administration secured legal cover through the OAS's Rio Treaty. On the evening of October 22, Kennedy addressed the nation and the world.

The days that followed gave no clean signal about whether the decision had been right. Soviet ships kept sailing toward the quarantine line. On October 27, a U.S. reconnaissance plane was shot down over Cuba and its pilot killed; that same day, aboard the Soviet submarine B-59 -- hunted by U.S. destroyers and cut off from Moscow -- officers argued over whether to fire a nuclear torpedo. Launch required all three senior officers to agree. One of them, Vasily Arkhipov, refused. No one in the White House knew, that day, that this had happened.

On October 28, Khrushchev announced by radio that he had agreed to withdraw the missiles. The United States publicly pledged not to invade Cuba, and secretly agreed to remove its own aging Jupiter missiles from Turkey -- an arrangement kept out of public view for years afterward.

Today the episode is often flattened into a story about a cool-headed Kennedy facing down a reckless Khrushchev. That flattening erases two things: that the U.S. side never had full control of events even as it made its choice, and that the Soviet concession was reciprocal, tied to a concession of Washington's own that stayed secret for a long time.

Going back to what Kennedy and ExComm actually knew at T0, the picture was incomplete in ways that mattered. They didn't know nuclear warheads had already reached Cuba. They underestimated Soviet troop strength on the island by a wide margin. Working inside that gap, the best available move was one that kept the door open to reversing course.

That's the distinction worth holding onto: decision quality versus outcome quality. The blockade itself was a carefully reasoned choice given what was knowable at the time -- it lowered the odds of runaway escalation and gave the other side an exit. On those terms, it's fair to call it a strong decision. But whether it actually ended without war also turned on things the White House neither planned for nor controlled -- Arkhipov's refusal chief among them. A good outcome doesn't prove the decision was flawless.

If you had been in that room, told the missiles might be operational within days, which would you have chosen -- strike or blockade? And if your choice hadn't led to war, would that have been entirely because of your judgment, or partly because of another judgment, made by someone else, somewhere you couldn't see?
